E. T. S.), l. 3380.}}}} '''wonder''' (wun′dėr), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wonder'', ''wondir'', ''wounder'', ''wunder'', ''wundur'', < AS. ''wundor'' = OS. ''wundar'' = D. ''wonder'' = MLG. ''wunder'' = OHG. ''wuntar'', MHG. G. ''wunder'' = Icel. ''undr'' (for *''vundr'') = Sw. Dan. ''under'', wonder; perhaps akin to Gr. ἀθρεῖν (*Ϝαθρεῖν?), gaze at.]   '''1.''' A strange thing; a cause of surprise, astonishment, or admiration; in a restricted sense, a miracle; a marvel, prodigy, or portent. {{smaller block|Whi thow wratthest the now ''wonder'' me thynketh. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), iii. 182.}}}} {{smaller block|The prophetis seiden with mylde steuene “A song of ''wondris'' now synge we.” {{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 52.}}}} {{smaller block|The love of boys unto their lords is strange; I have read ''wonders'' of it. {{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, ii. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|It is no ''wonder'' that art gets not the victory over nature. {{right|''Bacon'', Physical Fables, iv., Expl.}}}} {{smaller block|Bless me! Charles, you consúme more tea than all my family, though we are seven in the parlour, and as much sugar and butter — well, it ’s no ''wonder'' you are bilious! {{right|''Thackeray'', Lovel the Widower, ii.}}}} '''2.''' That emotion which is excited by novelty, or the presentation to the sight or mind of something new, unusual, strange, great, extraordinary, not well understood, or that arrests the attention by its novelty, grandeur, or inexplicableness. {{smaller|''Wonder'' expresses less than ''astonishment'', and much less than ''amazement''. It differs from ''admiration'' in not being necessarily accompanied with love, esteem, or approbation. But ''wonder'' sometimes is nearly allied to ''astonishment'', and the exact extent of the meaning of such words can hardly be graduated.}} {{smaller block|They were filled with ''wonder'' and amazement. {{right|Acts iii. 10.}}}} {{smaller block|O, how her eyes dart ''wonder'' on my heart! Mount bloode, soule to my lips, taste Hebe’s cup; Stande firme on decke, when beauties close-fight ’s up. {{right|''Marston'', Antonio and Mellida, I., i. 1.}}}} {{smaller block|''Wonder'' is the effect of novelty upon ignorance. {{right|''Johnson''.}}}} {{smaller block|The faculty of ''wonder'' is not defunct, but is only getting more and more emancipated from the unnatural service of terror, and restored to its proper function as a minister of delight. {{right|''Lowell'', Among my Books, 1st ser., p. 149.}}}} '''3.''' A cruller. [New Eng.] {{smaller block|A plate of crullers or ''wonders'', as a sort of sweet fried cake was commonly called. {{right|''H. B. Stowe'', The Minister’s Wooing, iv.}}}} {{smaller|'''Bird of wonder''', the phenix.—'''Nine days’ wonder''', a subject of astonishment and gossip for a short time, generally a petty scandal.}} {{smaller block|For when men han wel cryed, than wol they roune, Ek ''wonder'' last but ''nine nyght'' (var. ''days'') nevere in toune. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, iv. 588.}}}} So ran the tale like fire about the court, {{smaller block|Fire in dry stubble a ''nine days’ wonder'' flared. {{right|''Tennyson'', Lancelot and Elaine.}}}} {{smaller|'''Seven wonders of the world''', the seven most remarkable structures of ancient times. These were the Egyptian pyramids, the mausoleum erected by Artemisia at Halicarnassus, the temple of Artemis at Ephesus, the walls and hanging gardens of Babylon, the colossus at Rhodes, the statue of Zeus by Phidias in the great temple at Olympia, and the Pharos or lighthouse at Alexandria.—'''Wonder-making Parliament.''' Same as ''Merciless Parliament'' (which see, under ''parliament''). ='''Syn. 1.''' Sign, marvel, phenomenon, spectacle, rarity.—'''2.''' Surprise, bewilderment. See def. 2.}} '''wonder''' (wun′dėr), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wondren'', ''wondrien'', ''wundren'', < AS. ''wundrian'' = D. ''wonderen'' = MLG. ''wunderen'' = OHG. ''wuntarōn'', MHG. G. ''wundern'' = Icel. Sw. ''undra'' = Dan. ''undre'', wonder; from the noun.]   '''I.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be affected with wonder or surprise; marvel; be amazed: formerly with a reflexive dative. {{smaller block|Ac ''me wondreth'' in my witt whi that thei ne preche
As Paul the apostel prechede to the peuple ofte. {{right|''Piers Plowman'' (C), xvi. 74.}}}} {{smaller block|I ''wonder'' to see the contrarieties among the Papists. {{right|''Coryat'', Crudities, I. 41.}}}} {{smaller block|Who can but ''wonder'' at the fautors of these wonders? {{right|''Sandys'', Travailes, p. 160.}}}} {{smaller block|Here more then two hundred of those grim Courtiers stood ''wondering'' at him, as he had beene a monster; till Powhatan and his trayne had put themselues in their greatest braveries. {{right|Quoted in ''Capt. John Smith’s'' Works, I. 162.}}}} {{smaller block|We cease to ''wonder'' at what we understand. {{right|''Johnson.''}}}} '''2.''' To look with or feel admiration. {{smaller block|Nor did I ''wonder'' at the lily’s white. {{right|''Shak.'', Sonnets, xcviii.}}}} '''3.''' To entertain some doubt or curiosity in reference to some matter; speculate expectantly; be in a state of expectation mingled with doubt and slight anxiety or wistfulness: as, I ''wonder'' whether we shall reach the place in time: like to know.” {{smaller block|A boy or a child, ''I wonder?'' {{right|''Shak.'', W. T., iii. 3. 71.}}}} '''To be to be wondered†''', to be a cause for astonishment. {{smaller block|It ''is'' not ''to be wondered'' if Ben Jonson has many such lines as these. {{right|''Dryden.''}}}} {{smaller block|It ''is'' not ''to be wondered'' that we are shocked. {{right|''Defoe.''}}}} '''II.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To be curious about; wish to know; speculate in regard to: as, I ''wonder'' where John has gone. Like old acquaintance in a trance, Met far from home, ''wondering'' each other’s chance. {{smaller block|{{right|''Shak.'', Lucrece, l. 1596.}}}} {{smaller block|I have ''wondred'' these thirty yeares what Kings aile. {{right|''N. Ward'', Simple Cobler, p. 50.}}}} ''Wondering'' why that grief and rage and sin Was ever wrought. {{smaller block|{{right|''William Morris'', Earthly Paradise, II. 294.}}}} '''2.''' To surprise; amaze. [Rare.] {{smaller block|She has a sedateness that ''wonders'' me still more. {{right|''Mme. D’Arblay'', Diary, Oct. 25, 1788.}}}} '''wonder†''' (wun′dėr), ''a.''   [ME., an elliptical use of ''wonder'', ''n.'', as in comp.; cf. ''wonders''.]   Wonderful. Then sayde the pope, “Alas! Alas! Modur, this ys to me a ''wondur'' case.” {{smaller block|{{right|''Political Poems'', etc. (ed. Furnivall), p. 86.}}}} Allas! what is this ''wonder'' maladye? For hete of cold, for cold of hete, I dye. {{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, i. 419.}}}} '''wonder†''' (wun′dėr), ''adv.''   [ME., < ''wonder'', ''a.'']   Wonderfully; exceedingly; very. {{smaller block|Ye knowe eke that in form of speche is chaunge Withinne a thousand yere, and wordes tho That hadden prys, now ''wonder'' nyce and straunge Us thynketh hem. {{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 24.}}}} {{smaller block|''Wonder'' pale he waxe, wanting his colour, For ende hade he none of this grett doloure. {{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 2870.}}}} '''wondered†''' (wun′dėrd), ''a.''   [< ''wonder'' + ''-ed''2.]   Having performed wonders; able to produce wonders; wonderworking. [Rare.] {{smaller block|Let me live here ever; So rare a ''wonder’d'' father, and a wife, Makes this place Paradise. {{right|''Shak.'', Tempest, iv. 1. 123.}}}} '''wonderer''' (wun′dėr-ėr), ''n.''   [< ''wonder'' + ''-er''1.]   One who wonders. '''Wonderful''' (wun′dėr-fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wonderful, wonderfol, wundervol'' (= G. ''wundervoll''); < ''wonder'' + ''-ful''.]   Of a nature or kind to excite wonder or admiration; strange; astonishing; surprising; marvelous. {{smaller block|Who is he that hideth counsel without knowledge? therefore have I uttered that I understood not; things too ''wonderful'' for me, which I knew not. Job xlii. 3. Keep a gamester from the dice, and a good student from his book, and it is ''wonderful.'' {{right|''Shak.'', M. W. of W., iii. 1. 39.}}}} {{smaller block|They also shewed him some of the engines with which some of his servants had done ''wonderful'' things. {{right|''Bunyan'', Pilgrim’s Progress, i.}}}} '''Wonderful Parliament.''' {{smaller|Same as ''Merciless Parliament'' (which see, under ''parliament''). ='''Syn.''' ''Wonderful, Strange, Surprising, Curious, Unique,'' extraordinary, marvelous, amazing, startling, wondrous (poetic). ''Wonderful'' generally refers to something above the common, and so marvelous, perhaps almost incredible. ''Strange'' refers rather to something beside the common—that is, simply very unusual or odd, and so exciting surprise or wonder. Anything that excites awe or high admiration, or strikes one as sublime, is ''wonderful;'' an unpleasant object may be ''strange,'' but would not be called ''wonderful.'' That which is unexpected is ''surprising,'' but it is not necessarily ''strange:'' as, a ''surprising'' fact; a ''surprising'' discovery in science. ''Curious'' is ''wonderful'' on a small scale; by its derivation it often refers to an object extremely nice and intricate or elaborate in its details, but also it often conveys the notion of pleasing strangeness and even of rarity: as, a ''curious'' bit of mosaic; a ''curious'' piece of mechanism; a ''curiously'' colored stone. ''Unique'' expresses that which is sole of its kind or quality: as, a ''unique'' book; a ''unique'' sort of person. See ''eccentric'' and ''surprise.''}} '''wonderful''' (wun′dėr-fu̇l), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wonderfull;'' < ''wonderful, a.'']   Wonderfully; exceedingly; very. [Obsolete or vulgar.] Alas! she comyth ''wonderfull'' lyghtly; Man seith not the hour ne hou he shall dy. {{smaller block|{{right|''Rom. of Partenay'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 6159.}}}} {{smaller block|Chymistry, I know by a little Experience, is ''wonderful'' easing. {{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. vi. 41.}}}} '''nderfully''' (wun′dėr-fu̇l-i), ''adv.''   [< ME. ''wonrfully''; < ''wonderful'' + ''-ly''2.]   '''1.''' In a wonrful manner; in a manner to excite wonder surprise; surprisingly; strangely; remarkly: in colloquial language often nearly or ite equivalent to ‘very’: as, ''wonderfully'' lit- difference. {{smaller block|ȝe schal se him rise vp and speke, and ''wondirfully'' be nfortid and strenkthid therby. {{right|''Book of Quinte Essence'' (ed. Furnivall), p. 15.}}}} {{smaller block|will praise thee; for I am fearfully and ''wonderfully'' de. {{right|Ps. cxxxix. 14.}}}}
